blocks.content: The High Court stands at the head of a state's judicial administration.

rows: Apex judicial body for the entire country
Head of the judicial administration in a State
Wider: Enforces Fundamental Rights and legal rights (Art. 226)

items: High Courts derive their authority directly from the Constitution and are not administratively subordinate to the Supreme Court.
Article 214 mandates a High Court for each state, but Parliament possesses exclusive power under Article 231 to establish a common High Court.
Extending or excluding the jurisdiction of a High Court over any Union Territory can only be done by Parliament through federal legislation.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: In the Indian single integrated judicial system, the High Court operates below the Supreme Court but stands at the apex of the state judicial administration.
Part VI of the Constitution, from Articles 214 to 231, deals with the organization, independence, jurisdiction, powers, and procedures of the High Courts.
The institution of the High Court originated in India in 1862 when High Courts were established at Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras under the High Courts Act of 1861.
The 7th Constitutional Amendment Act of 1956 authorized Parliament to establish a common High Court for two or more states or for two or more states and a Union Territory.
